title: The New Kid Can't Find the Way

steps.title: Lost Between Classrooms!
steps.story: Kian has just started at a big new school. The corridors all look the same, and he keeps getting lost on the way to art, music and the lunch hall. Every time, he arrives late and a bit worried. Can YOU design a way-finding system that any new kid could follow, first time?

steps.prompt: Do you already have an idea for helping someone find their way in a new place?

steps.intro: How does nature find the way home? Some animals travel huge distances and still find the exact spot they started from. Let's follow them!

clues.text: A desert ant walks far from its nest on the hot, flat sand, where there are almost no landmarks. It counts its steps and uses the sun as a compass, then walks in a straight line home.
A honeybee remembers landmarks, like a tall tree, a pond or a red flower bed, and uses them to fly back to the hive and to flowers it visited before.
A sea turtle can feel Earth's magnetism, like having a compass inside. Years later, females swim thousands of kilometres back to lay eggs near the beach where they hatched.
A salmon remembers the smell of the stream where it hatched. After years at sea, it follows that smell upstream to find its home stream again.

steps.secret: Use more than one clue! The heroes use landmarks, counting, direction and smell, and the clues back each other up. If one fails, like the sun going behind a cloud, another one still works. Good way-finding systems for people do the same: signs, colours, maps, arrows and landmarks all tell the same story, so nobody gets lost if they miss one.
steps.reveal_hint: Which 2 or 3 different kinds of clues could your system use, so a new kid still finds the way if they miss one?

steps.instructions: Pick a route at home with at least 3 turns, like from the front door to your bed via the kitchen. Guide a family member along it 4 different ways: spoken words only, a drawn map, coloured paper arrows, and landmarks ('turn left at the plant'). Count their wrong turns each time. Which way worked best?
hints: Use the same route and the same helper each time, so only the clue type changes. Swap the order you try them in, or they'll learn the route!
Landmarks work best when they are big and different, like 'the blue door' or 'the tall plant', not 'the third door'. Doors often look the same.

steps.prompt: Draw a map of your route and your way-finding system.
steps.guidance: Mark each decision point, where someone could go the wrong way. Show which clues you'll put there, like a colour line, an arrow, a landmark or a step count.

steps.instructions: Build your way-finding system along a route at home, or at school with a teacher's OK. Use paper arrows, coloured tape or string lines, landmark signs and a pocket map. Then ask someone who has never done the route to follow it without your help. Count their wrong turns. Take photos of your signs only, not of people.
test_criteria: How many wrong turns did your tester make?
At which decision point did they hesitate or go wrong?
Improve one thing and test again with a new tester. Add a second clue at the tricky spot. Were there fewer wrong turns?
hints: Watch where your tester slows down or stops. That's the exact spot that needs a better clue.
Use the desert ant and honeybee trick together: one colour line to follow all the way, plus a big landmark sign at every turn. Two clues at each turn beat one.

steps.celebration_text: Kian walks from class to class without getting lost, and now he helps the next new kid find the way! Your system works like a bee's landmarks and an ant's compass.
steps.share_prompt: Share a photo of your map or signs and your tester's wrong turns on the Ideas Wall. Which clue helped most?

age_tier_variants.summary: Test which clues help people follow a route, then design a way-finding system with more than one kind of clue and test it with a new tester.
Explain path integration and landmark navigation, design a system with redundant cues, measure wrong turns and hesitation points, and compare with signage in airports and hospitals.
